records.c: Bytes preceding the $0810 entry. The instruction fragment calls $E5A0, sets the processor port to $35 and clears the VIC border colour.
Initializes each fighter's $781A/$781B value to 200 minus its training byte at $CE17/$CE18, modulo 256. Selects separate initialization paths for one and two apprentices using $CE00.
Restores VIC-II settings, sets video bank $0000 and selects the $0400 screen and $2000 bitmap. Calls $EC68 with the scene index and chooses the outcome or fight setup using $CD59.

Selects the descriptor bank using the facing flag at $780E and looks up the pose through $7DCF. Adds $B500 to the relative pointer and distributes eight or sixteen bytes to the alternating display buffers.

Called by the $1E93 raster phase. Toggles $7819 on each call and services the bars on alternating calls. Signed pending changes at $7817 and $7818 move the positions two pixels at a time, subject to the respective bounds.
Uses the low three position bits to select a mask and the upper bits to target an eight-byte bitmap cell at $3E00. Clears masked bits before decrementing the position twice.
Masks eight bytes from the first stored bar at $4B00 and writes them to the matching bitmap cell at $3E00.
Uses the low three position bits to select a mask and the upper bits to target an eight-byte cell at $3EA0. Clears masked bits before incrementing the position twice.
Masks eight bytes from the second stored bar at $4BA0 and writes them to the matching bitmap cell at $3EA0.
Reads the name at $7896 up to $FF. Converts each byte to a glyph offset in RAM beneath I/O and copies its eight pixel rows into the bitmap beginning at $2000.
Returns if the opponent move-state offset is nonzero. Chooses a boundary from the facing and move ID. At the left limit, marks the move offset idle with $FF.
Checks the active opponent move and horizontal position. When the applicable left threshold is crossed, sets X to eight, selects pose zero and sets the motion offset to idle $FF.
Looks up the right boundary for the opponent’s move as a two-byte coordinate. The move idles if the opponent is at or beyond that boundary.
Checks the high X byte, facing and move state for an edge transition. The reset path puts the opponent at $0118, clears its current pose and sets the motion offset to idle $FF.
Selects an edge test from the apprentice facing and move. The left test uses the table at $7D6F and sets the move offset to idle $FF when the boundary test succeeds.
Checks the apprentice position and permitted move state. The left reset sets X to eight and puts the apprentice in the idle pose.
Looks up the apprentice’s movement limit through $7D7D. If its 16-bit X position reaches that limit, marks the movement offset idle.
Checks apprentice X, facing and move state, then restores the idle pose and horizontal position $0118 when the edge condition passes.
Checks training unlock flags for moves four, six and seven. Reads an action script from $7AE7 and dispatches its joystick checks and movement or attack commands. Values below $64 select poses.
Subtracts $64 from the script command to select a signed horizontal delta. Uses one of two facing-dependent tables and adds it to the opponent position before advancing the script.
Interprets command bytes $C8–$CD as comparisons with the saved stick sample. The result can advance, hold or restart the script. Some branches recheck an edge or shift the opponent by eight pixels.
Writes twice the pose number to $7FA0. Loads the signed horizontal offset from the current facing table and saves it in $780A/$780B.
Calls the first contact handler for script command $CE, then advances the script.
Checks the second training unlock fields for moves four, six and seven. Uses the same action-script directory with its own progress byte.
Converts a command from $64 upward to a horizontal delta from the active facing table. Adds it to the apprentice position and resumes the script.
Implements the hold, advance or restart decisions for script commands $C8–$CD using the other stick sample. Selected branches recheck edge conditions or shift the apprentice by eight pixels.
Writes twice the pose number to $788C. Reads the signed horizontal pose offset from the active facing table and saves it in $7808/$7809.
Calls the second contact handler when the interpreter reaches $CE, then resumes the script.
Stages the first fighter index and facing flag before jumping to the common shape address calculation.
Stages the second fighter index and its own facing flag, and then jumps to the same shape address calculation.

Builds the output pointer from the supplied position and backing-plane offsets. Looks up the shape through a relative word at $8000 and uses its two dimension bytes before dispatching to the appropriate painter.
Selects the blend path according to facing. Applies the pixel mask lookup when combining the packed fighter rows with the destination.
Selects the row copying path according to the second fighter facing bit. Advances the bitmap destination by $140 per row and the source by the packed row width.
Clears the bitmap destination at $2000 and the auxiliary plane beginning at $5180 using overlapping page writes.
Acknowledges VIC interrupts, saves registers and advances the phase byte at $7867. The fifth service resets the phase byte and takes the common CIA acknowledge and register-restore path.
Times the first background colour change with NOPs, sets $D016 to $18 and reads the colour and next raster compare from the selected scene state.
After a shorter NOP delay, writes the second background colour and schedules the compare at line $A1.

Writes the third background colour and switches the VIC bank and display layout according to $786C. Applies pending sprite-zero positions, saves $FA–$FF across the SID and score drawing calls, then schedules line $EE.
Waits for raster line $F1, increments the game tick count at $7816, restores the main bitmap bank and schedules line $FF.
Writes $08 to the horizontal display control, services the two bars through $0F0D and schedules line $39.

Indexes the ten-byte descriptors at $7832 with the scene index in A. Reads the stream backwards and handles literal, run, pointer reset and exit tokens. Writes the selected bitmap and screen-colour plane.
Banks out ROM and I/O to read the source at ($58),Y. Decrements the 16-bit input pointer, restores the ROM mapping and preserves X.
Banks out ROM and I/O to write A through ($5A),Y. Decrements the 16-bit output pointer and restores the ROM mapping.
Copies the first row from $78BF and the lower rows from $4C40 and $4C54. Fills the colour RAM and initializes the screen and work copies of the lower display.
Matches the title glyph data from $0A45 through $0A7F byte for byte. The Combat introduction copies its displayed font from $DC80.
Compressed background for combat scene 3, source offsets 1705–2728 measured back from $4AA8. The decoder reads backwards and reconstructs the screen matrix and bitmap.
Compressed background for combat scene 3, source offsets 681–1704 measured back from $4AA8. The decoder reads backwards and reconstructs the screen matrix and bitmap.
Compressed background for combat scene 3, source offsets 0–680 measured back from $4AA8. The decoder reads backwards and reconstructs the screen matrix and bitmap.
Twenty 8-byte bitmap cells for the first lower bar. $0FB7 reads a cell selected by the upper position bits, masks it, and copies it to $3E00 plus the cell offset.

Twenty 8-byte bitmap cells for the second lower bar. $1002 reads from this plane and writes the masked cell to $3EA0 plus the cell offset. The first eight bytes are zero, below the lowest cell the reveal path reads.
Two 21-cell strips of bitmap colour pairs. The first ends at the shared cell $4C54 where the second starts. $1F52 copies them to $07C0 and $07D4.
Fifteen trailing HUD colour-cell values following the 41 bytes selected by the HUD initializer.
The weapon setup at $0E0D stores pointer $7D for sprite zero. In VIC bank $4000 that pointer selects the slot at $5F40.
Eight groups with three bytes per sprite row. The reflected attack-mask painter writes the first two bytes in each row and preserves the third.
Zero-filled lower part of the 64-byte weapon sprite at $5F40. The mask writer supplies the upper rows and pointer $7D selects the full sprite slot.

Fighter positions, headings, action indices and contact state, plus the two staggered timing counters and the HUD bar endpoints.
Four ten-byte scene descriptors selected at $1E9E. Each supplies the descending input and output pointers, the marker and the following scene parameters.

Stick samples and per-fighter action counters followed by bitmap painter state. The painters store the active source address, width, height and previous draw bounds in this area.
The editable text fields filled from the two resident apprentice names. The font stamper reads positioned glyphs beginning at $7896.
Trailing text bytes of the second name record. The following 40-byte pattern is the HUD’s lower screen colour row.
Forty screen-colour bytes copied to $0400–$0427, the first matrix row, by $1F52.
One mask for each possible source byte. A zero two-bit pixel gives mask bits 11, and a coloured pixel gives 00. The painter ANDs the background with this byte before ORing the source.
One byte for each possible source byte. Reverses the four two-bit pixels within the byte for the reflected fighter painter.

Nine signed 16-bit horizontal deltas used for the opposite facing. The script command selects the same delta index.
Ninety-three pairs reached by doubling the pose number. The script painter picks this table for one facing and uses the pair as the fighter’s relative horizontal position.
Ninety-three position-offset pairs for the other facing, selected by the same pose number.

Action comparison values read by the second contact guard.
Calculated horizontal position and vertical placement for the weapon overlay. $0C64 seeds the X value from the fighter position and adds the selected pose offset.

Two bytes per pose for the forward weapon placement. The first advances the fighter X position and the second sets the weapon Y position.
Two bytes per pose for the opposite weapon placement. The first is a signed horizontal adjustment and the second sets Y.
The active opponent frame number multiplied by two. The animator writes this at $170C and the painter reads it at $0C2B.

Beginning of frame 82, with a two-byte header of $07,$20. Its declared pixels extend beyond $C2FF into the live exit routine.
Blanks the screen, mutes the SID, restores the ROM and KERNAL vectors and loads HIGH from device 8 before returning to BASIC run.
The four-byte name HIGH passed to KERNAL SETNAM by the combat exit.
At raster $FF, sets border and background to black and blanks the display. Returns after 100 successful reads of raster line zero.
Waits for raster line zero and sets $D011 to $3B to enable the bitmap display.
Sets the KERNAL input and output device numbers to 0 and 3. Copies the VIC-II preset from $ECB9, leaving display control, border and background colour unchanged.
Pixel bytes after the display setup that starts inside the nominal frame 83 allocation at $C336. The frame pointer resolves into instruction bytes before these pixels.
Zero-filled space before the opponent control routine. The oversized frame 83 render samples $C4D0 as a pixel source when it interprets the instruction bytes at $C336 as dimensions.
Checks both move states. The idle or blocked path sets the opponent’s synthetic stick to $FF and primes its timers, otherwise continues to the spacing check.

Subtracts the fighter X positions and stores a magnitude and side. With a low distance byte of at least $64, switches the facing selector, sets the spacing threshold from CIA timer bits and requests $FE.
Checks the current player move, retreat latch and distance. The reposition path sets $FE and changes the facing selector according to positional limits at X=$58 and $C9.
Starts from a directional command based on facing. Checks the player action and compares CIA timer bits with $7800 to decide whether to try a move-specific reaction.
Compares the player move with seven candidate action IDs and tests the matching distance condition. Selects a synthetic stick code for the reactions that pass.

Within the stored distance threshold, decrements the wait timer. A negative result sets the reposition latch and reaches the command-return path with the previously stored command. While the timer is nonnegative, the CIA timer and threshold at $7801 choose the next decision path.
Samples three bits of the CIA timer. Uses those bits, distance bands and facing to select a synthetic stick command, then stores it for the opponent action code.
Masks the CIA timer with $11 and fetches a command from $C774. Normalizes a zero command to idle $FF before returning.
Eighteen synthetic stick bytes. The $11 mask in the caller selects positions 0, 1, 16 or 17.
Distance and side bytes, decision delays, the reposition latch and the three separately masked CIA timer bits used by the opponent move picker.
Fourteen bytes after the last opponent decision field. Loaded nonzero cells at $C793, $C795–$C796, $C798 and $C79E are retained beside the decision variables.
Zero-filled space after opponent control and before the score painter. The frame 83 renderer samples $C810, $C8E0 and $C9B0 from this range as pixels.

Alternates the two displayed scores using $CD4B. Formats five decimal digits and writes eight bytes per glyph from RAM beneath I/O into the upper bitmap row. Restores the processor port after drawing.
Starts with five PETSCII zero digits and accumulates a five-digit contribution for each of the four nibbles in the score word at $CB80.
Adds the selected five-byte decimal string from the units end, carrying left whenever a PETSCII digit reaches $3A. The caller patches the source operand before each call.
Byte-for-byte copy of the title’s fast-loader code in the range that the Combat score painter partly overlays. Includes the serial close, LOAD vector restoration and final-block reader.
The score painter copies the current score here from $CE1F or $CE21 according to the alternating selector.
Five PETSCII digits produced by $CA96. $CA48 reads each digit as a glyph selector.
Sixteen pointers indexed by score nibble 0, which is the coefficient of 1. Each points to a five-digit decimal string.
Sixteen pointers indexed by score nibble 1, which is the coefficient of 16. Each points to a five-digit decimal string.
Sixteen pointers indexed by score nibble 2, which is the coefficient of 256. Each points to a five-digit decimal string.
Sixteen pointers indexed by score nibble 3, which is the coefficient of 4096. Each points to a five-digit decimal string.
Sixteen five-character decimal strings for multiples of 1, from zero to 15. The carry routine adds one string from this table to the digit buffer.
Sixteen five-character decimal strings for multiples of 16, from zero to 240. The carry routine adds one string from this table to the digit buffer.
Sixteen five-character decimal strings for multiples of 256, from zero to 3840. The carry routine adds one string from this table to the digit buffer.
Sixteen five-character decimal strings for multiples of 4096, from zero to 61440. The carry routine adds one string from this table to the digit buffer.
Four scratch offsets written by the score formatter. Low byte nibbles come first, each multiplied by two to index the relevant decimal contribution pointers.
Toggles on each call to $CA00 and selects the next score field and screen offset to update.
Scene number, interlude selector and result state used when choosing which presentation to draw.
Space and PETSCII SHI DE YU in the ten bytes preceding the interlude exit flag.
When this byte is one after the interlude, Combat jumps to the disk exit for HIGH.
Little-endian score amounts indexed by the move. The contact handlers add the selected word and adjust it with the apprentice’s training values.
Byte-for-byte copy of this section of the title disk receiver’s fill bytes and CIA2 input mask table.
Zero-filled remainder of the loader area. The oversized Combat frame 83 includes a pixel read at $CDC0.
Compressed background for combat scene 0, source offsets 1903–2926 measured back from $DB6E. The decoder reads backwards and reconstructs the screen matrix and bitmap.
Compressed background for combat scene 0, source offsets 879–1902 measured back from $DB6E. The decoder reads backwards and reconstructs the screen matrix and bitmap.
Compressed background for combat scene 0, source offsets 0–878 measured back from $DB6E. The decoder reads backwards and reconstructs the screen matrix and bitmap.
The three-page glyph source for the combat introduction, read from the RAM beneath I/O and copied to the character generator at $2000.
Jumps to the voice service entry at $E0B2.
Clears the voice and filter state and resets the SID. Uses A to select the divider and six initial voice pointer bytes, and marks the first pass to fetch a sequence entry.
Interprets track bytes as a new track pointer, voice offsets or a repeat count. Nonnegative values select a phrase through the directory. Saves the new track position and begins the phrase.
Starts the player at voice index two or continues the current voice. The tick divider and note timers decide whether to fetch another phrase byte or step the instrument and write the active voice.
Selects the phrase using the current voice’s index. Decodes note, duration, instrument, filter, pitch override and slide commands. A zero byte returns to track processing.
Updates SID gate and envelope according to the instrument flags, resets modulation on a new note and reads the note frequency from its two byte tables. Updates the duration and saved phrase position.

Services the remaining voices by descending register index. The final voice updates the tick divider and SID mode and resonance. The filter step path reads a timed incremental cutoff command and writes $D416.

Initializes the slide when its counter is negative. Computes the interval from the difference of two note frequencies divided by the duration. Thereafter decrements the counter and adds the stored interval.
Writes a relative note lookup or a literal high frequency byte, then resumes instrument decoding. The silent branch resets the selected voice control and both envelope registers before moving on.
Uses the current instrument or the active override to select a pitch program. Applies its loop and timing fields and updates the note frequency from the program’s command.
Uses the instrument to choose a timed pulse increment program and advances that program when the countdown elapses. Adds the active increment to the saved pulse width.
Selects a fixed instrument control byte or the next byte from a control program. Applies the current voice mask and saves the program position.
Writes control, frequency, pulse width, attack/decay and sustain/release to the selected SID voice, then advances to the next voice.
Twenty-two eight-byte instrument records. The player indexes their envelope, control and modulation fields with the selected instrument number times eight.
Split low and high pitch program pointers and their loop limits and positions. The override path writes the element at index zero of each array.
Arrays of low and high pointers based at $E5FD and $E608. The pulse driver uses the nonzero selector from the instrument byte.
Split pointers to sequences of SID control bytes and their loop restart offsets. The instrument supplies the sequence length and selector.
Filter program pointers from the tables based at $E628 and $E62A, followed by the control values indexed from $E62C.
Override table entries for pointer low bytes, high bytes, length and loop position. The player copies the selected values into index zero of the ordinary pitch directory.
Short pitch programs selected by the override directory. Their entries provide the note offsets and control bytes for $E3A5.
Embedded message about Revolution, followed by the MIC/AD and F.A.M.E. attribution and 1989 date.
records.d: THERE WILL ONLY EVER BE ONE REVO

records.c: Ninety-five low bytes of SID frequencies, read during note changes and the pitch slide calculation.
Embedded tune credit for the arrangement of G’D Old Scotch. It sits between the two frequency tables.
records.d: G'D OLD SCOTCH BY MIC/AD OF F.A.

records.c: Ninety-five high bytes of SID frequencies, paired by note with the table at $E6C0.
The offsets 0, 7 and 14 for the three SID register groups.
Voice and filter state cleared by $E003. Holds frequency, instrument index, control and modulation positions, track pointers and the tick divider.
Fifteen little-endian phrase pointers selected by doubling the active track’s phrase index. Some phrase entry points are inside other streams.
Three voice track low bytes, three high bytes and the initial music tick divider for tune zero.
The pitch, pulse, control and filter programs reached from the split pointer tables. The short command streams provide modulation delays, increments and loop positions.
Embedded credit naming AD Bulka as the music code author.
First SID voice track sequence. Its final $FF and pointer restart it at $E939, one byte after its initial phrase.
Second SID voice track sequence. Its phrase indices and repeat command feed the track interpreter at $E047.
Third SID voice track sequence, ending with $FF and the restart pointer $E96F.
Phrase bytes reached by directory indices zero through nine. Some note and duration commands are shared by multiple directory pointers.
Phrase bytes reached by directory indices ten through fourteen. This group contains the higher-index sections of the tune and shares the decoder at $E0D4.
Waits for CIA1 port A to equal $6F. A different reading clears the latch at $CE23, and accepting a press sets the latch so a held button cannot count twice.
Clears the screen, builds the bordered interlude from the shared templates at $CF00 and chooses its text through $CD4D. Shows it until fire, then blanks the display.
Selects a sequence of text IDs through $EE4A. Passes each to $ECFF until encountering $FF.
Selects a message pointer through $EE6D, uses its row and column to find screen RAM, translates capital letters to screen codes and handles $FE and $FF delimiters.
Places character RAM at $2000 and the matrix at $0400. Banks out I/O while reading the font at $DC80 and then programs the display colours.
The 25 row offsets from the $0400 screen base, in increments of 40. The renderer at $ED0B adds the column from each text row to the selected offset.
Seven list pointers. The presentation at $EC68 uses the event at $CD4D to choose one through $ECD7.
Interlude event 0 requests positioned messages 0 and 7. The $FF byte returns from the list loop.
Interlude event 1 requests positioned messages 1 and 7. The $FF byte returns from the list loop.
Interlude event 2 requests positioned messages 2 and 8. The $FF byte returns from the list loop.
Interlude event 3 requests positioned messages 3 and 8. The $FF byte returns from the list loop.
Interlude event 4 requests positioned messages 4 and 8. The $FF byte returns from the list loop.
Interlude event 5 requests positioned messages 5 and 8. The $FF byte returns from the list loop.
Interlude event 6 requests positioned messages 6 and 7. The $FF byte returns from the list loop.
Nine message pointers indexed by the list bytes through $ECFF. Each target starts with a column and row.
Message 0 draws "YOU HAVE BEEN / DEFEATED!" at the column and row prefixed to each row. $FE introduces another positioned row and $FF ends the message.

Message 1 draws "CONGRATULATION! / YOU HAVE BEEN / VICTORIOUS / AGAINST THE ELITE / FIGHTERS OF SHAOLIN!" at the column and row prefixed to each row. $FE introduces another positioned row and $FF ends the message.
Message 2 draws "YOU BEGIN YOUR FIGHT / AT THE BOTTOM OF THE / MOUNTAINS!" at the column and row prefixed to each row. $FE introduces another positioned row and $FF ends the message.
Message 3 draws "WELL DONE! / YOUR SECOND FIGHT IS HELD / IN THE OLD PART OF THE / TOWN!" at the column and row prefixed to each row. $FE introduces another positioned row and $FF ends the message.
Message 4 draws "IMPRESSIVE! / NOW PROVE YOURSELF / ON THE MARKETPLACE OF / THE CITY!" at the column and row prefixed to each row. $FE introduces another positioned row and $FF ends the message.
Message 5 draws "BRILLIANT! / BUT NOW THE BEST FIGHTER / AWAITS YOU / BY THE CITYWALLS!" at the column and row prefixed to each row. $FE introduces another positioned row and $FF ends the message.
Message 6 draws "YOUR TRAINING IS OVER!" at the column and row prefixed to each row. $FE introduces another positioned row and $FF ends the message.
Message 7 draws "PUSH FIRE-BUTTON TO GO ON" at the column and row prefixed to each row. $FE introduces another positioned row and $FF ends the message.
Message 8 draws "PUSH FIRE-BUTTON TO START" at the column and row prefixed to each row. $FE introduces another positioned row and $FF ends the message.
Trailing little-endian offsets identical to the active directory slice at $F55C–$F647. The interlude text occupies the preceding addresses.
Retained duplicate of the graphics descriptor bytes at $F648–$F8FF, including the width-tagged weapon masks.
Page identical to the active weapon descriptor directory at $F500–$F5FF. The painter indexes the copy at $F500.
Eighty-two relative pointers to the first set of fighter display descriptors, selected with the facing flag clear. The code at $0CF8 adds $B500.
Eighty-two relative pointers into the second set of fighter display descriptors, selected with the facing flag set. These share the same $B500 base.
Beginning of the high-memory weapon shape pool. The entry data includes eight- and sixteen-pixel-byte masks consumed by the weapon painter.
Combat first display descriptor set, offsets 0–1023. The second byte of each record is the eight- or sixteen-byte body size read by $0D07.
Combat first display descriptor set, offsets 1024–1155. The second byte of each record is the eight- or sixteen-byte body size read by $0D07.
Combat second display descriptor set, offsets 0–1011. The second byte of each record is the eight- or sixteen-byte body size read by $0D07.
Retained helper instruction bytes. Tests $98, adds A to the pointer at $25/$26 with carry propagation and decrements X before returning.
Retained code that copies a VIC preset to $D000, copies a page fragment to $033F and writes a sprite pointer and a VIC bank value before jumping to $FFEA.
Sequence beginning with SEI and CLD that saves stack values into $DEFB–$DEFD and builds new stack values before jumping to $FECB.
Two short sequences that clear or set processor-port bit 1, changing the KERNAL ROM mapping.
Retained bytes include a SAMMER text fragment followed by the final hardware vector values. Combat writes its own IRQ vector when enabling the raster interrupt.
